ai_summary: Scotland's clean electricity generation presents a stark operational contrast to the wider network today. Total GB wind output reaches 9.7 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 3.8 GW, which represents 37.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Underpinned by this substantial volume of renewable generation, Scottish carbon intensity has reached 0 gCO2/kWh, outperforming the 113 gCO2/kWh recorded GB-wide. Nevertheless, transmission constraints between regions prevent the full integration and dispatch of this clean power across Great Britain. As a direct consequence of cross-border grid limitations, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has mounted to 1848.9 MWh, accumulating a constraint cost of about £49,372. To replace this blocked output and maintain grid stability elsewhere on the network, carbon-intensive thermal generators were dispatched, leading to an estimated gas burned elsewhere to replace it of 351291.0 m3. This displacement generated 647.1 tonnes CO2 in avoidable emissions. These system metrics illustrate the operational friction between local zero-carbon abundance and network capacity, highlighting how structural transmission bottlenecks simultaneously elevate consumer balancing expenses and dilute the broader emissions benefits of Scottish wind power.
